text:
I’ve taught students in special ed resource, K-8 classroom & children w/visual impairments. Over the years, I’ve noticed that some of the most critical learning doesn’t happen in the classroom—it comes from life experiences & the environment a child grows up, plays & learns in.
These experiences lay the foundation for understanding & applying classroom concepts. They build the kind of background knowledge that helps students connect ideas, understand analogies, & draw relationships between what they’re learning & the world around them.
Too often, the stories we read or the math word problems we give assume a level of real-world experience that many of today’s children just don’t have. How many middle schoolers today truly know how to tell time—not just digitally, but on an analog clock & in different ways? How many parents explain fractions using a Friday night pizza or bake w/their children & explain fractions on measuring cups? How many children know how to ride a bike, or understand how a river flows & ebbs —what a riverbank is—not the kind that holds money?  Many kids are dumbfounded by the concept of ratios or the odds of something happening? Use the concept of the weather or the lottery to pre-teach this skill. Our ed system has its flaws, but this problem goes deeper than that. It’s also about a lack of prior knowledge & a growing inability among children to think independently & apply what they know. We can’t rely on McMahon to make policy decisions—esp. since she can’t tell the diff btwn AI & A1 or what the Ed. acronyms mean. So, parents must step up— Go outside w/ your kids— take them camping— teach directions - teach how to read a clock, ride a bike, watch a river ebb & flow. Give them life to pull from when they sit down to learn. Be their 1st life skills teacher & your children will love it! ❤

author: @JJFlores197
text:
I work in K-12 IT. In my nearly 4.5 years there, I have seen a disgusting amount of waste in just about every category you can think of. Every school district is different, but I'd say the top administrators take up a non-negligible amount in salaries and benefits. And some of these admins don't directly work with students very much or at all or are even in the schools seeing the day-to-day activities of how schools run. Not saying their jobs aren't important, but a lot of them have bloated salaries relative to what they do.

I also see what I believe is a lack of accountability and vetting when it comes to purchasing. A few years ago at one of my schools, I found a printer that was still brand new in box. It was purchased around 2017 but for some reason, it was never put in use. It just sat hidden under a bunch of junk that piled over the years collecting dust. The thing cost at least $500 new. That's just 1 of many egregious examples of financial mismanagement.

My mom works at the school cafeteria. She likes the job but dislikes the disgusting amount of food waste every single day. They don't cook much food in-house as its mostly pre-packaged stuff that they warm up. The official policy is that anything that is left over gets thrown straight into the trash. No one is allowed to take any home or give it to other people. The kids are "forced" to take what's a complete meal which includes a main entree, veggies, fruit, and a milk carton. That is so it counts as a full meal so the district gets reimbursed for it. Lunch ladies are required to tell the kids that they HAVE to take a complete meal. If the kid doesn't want green beans for instance, they're still required to take it but they get old they can throw it in the trash. Its "ok" because at that point, the student already received a "complete" meal. Its absolute insanity. And the people in charge don't care. Its not their money nor is it the district's money. Its all business stuff so the food service dept has special funding from different sources so they don't care at all.

My aunt works in the pre-school system of that same district and its the same issue. Each year, the pre-school (child development program) gets a certain amount of funding. They allocate part of that funding for each pre-school classroom district-wide. Whether or not they need stuff, they have to buy stuff by a certain time. Every year, my aunt and her co-workers have to throw out stuff to make room for new furniture or toys or supplies because they have to use that money. They throw out stuff that's not even a year old and is in otherwise good condition to make room for more junk. Its a never ending cycle.

author: @ganzveruckt
text: After 36 years of teaching, I feel that you have it backwards: the education system isn't failing America, but rather America is failing both the students and the education system. As a teacher, you can try your best, but you're limited, because you have to work with what comes through your classroom door: the students. And those students are the product of their families. Close-knit, healthy, functional families that spend quality time with their kids produce kids who come through the classroom door wanting to learn. They're happy, polite, and have decent values & work ethics. They're easy and fun to teach. However, kids who come through that door from families that are 'too busy' to really give their undivided time to their kids produce kids that couldn't care less about learning. They're not really happy kids. They see little value in school, so they don't care about studying, doing homework, or the other things that require a little effort. For me, my 'teaching' was often just listening to those unhappy kids pour out their frustrations and sadness in my office, as they didn't have anyone else to lean on. So, yeah, I had kids from both ends of the spectrum, and in both cases, they were the best part of the job, the only real reward for becoming a teacher. On several occasions I bawled my eyes out at the heartbreak of suicidal students; however, on the other hand, sometimes felt thankful for having the privilege of helping student get excited about learning an idea or kids who kids who later thanked me for them getting accepted to universities; it was all part of being a teacher, the good and the bad. The pay was low, the hours always included evenings and weekends, but the rewards from the kids were great. You can blame the schools and teachers for 'failing' students' all you want, but, at the expense of generalizing, I would turn that around: much of modern American society is failing its students. Good or bad, it starts with the family, not the teacher.
